claim: Alt+G, Alt+R, and Alt+S reset an object's location, rotation, and scale respectively back to their default (unmodified) values -- ALT-modified versions of the plain G/R/S move/rotate/scale shortcuts.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript [58:21-58:35]: 'You probably know there are shortcuts, G for moving, R for rotating and S for scaling. And if you combine these shortcuts with ALT, ALT + G, R and S, you can reset the location rotation and scaling of the object.'
rejected_alternative: Manually re-entering 0 location / identity rotation / scale-1 values field by field in the N-panel for each axis.
reason: A single-keystroke-per-channel reset avoids slow, typo-prone manual transform-field edits when clearing accidental or exploratory transforms during iterative modeling.

claim: Enabling the Move tool's 'Origins' option (in the tool's Options at the top of the viewport) redirects G/R/S and any active snapping mode to transform only the object's origin instead of the whole object, so the origin can be repositioned (e.g. snapped to an edge center) without moving the mesh; disabling the option afterward resumes normal whole-object transforms.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript [59:37-1:00:10]: 'In order to change this, you can enable the move tool and up here under options, you can enable origin. Now you can simply move the origin wherever you want... You can even combine it with any snapping tool, for example, snap to edge center... when you're done with positioning your origin, you can simply disable this option up here, so you can move the whole object once again.'
rejected_alternative: Placing the 3D cursor first and using Set Origin > Origin to 3D Cursor as the only way to reposition an origin, or the Shift+Ctrl+Alt+C origin menu.
reason: An off-center or misplaced origin skews rotation/scale pivots and any later animation; this gives direct, snap-capable manual control over origin placement using the same transform tools already used on the object itself.

claim: In a parent-child hierarchy, enabling the Move tool's 'Parents' option (Options, top of viewport) lets the parent object be transformed (e.g. G, Z) without dragging its children along with it -- for correcting a parent's own position/rotation after children have already been placed relative to it.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript [1:00:28-1:00:54]: 'Now I wanna move it up without moving all the child objects, which is not possible right now, in order to do that, you have to go to options up here and click on parents. This means if I press G and Z, I now can move the parent without affecting the children. so I can move it up a bit until it fits, and then I simply disable this option here and now the parent works as expected.'
rejected_alternative: Un-parenting the children with Keep Transform, moving the parent, then re-parenting -- or manually counter-moving every child object by the same offset to cancel out the parent's move.
reason: Preserves an established parent-child grouping while still allowing the parent's own transform to be corrected in isolation -- relevant to any multi-part assembly or rig built with this project's Model/low-poly collection pairing.

claim: To snap an object flush onto a target's curved surface with correct orientation while moving it interactively, combine three settings: enable Face snapping, enable 'Align Rotation to Target' (rotates the object's local Z to match the surface normal), and enable 'Project Individual Elements'. With only Face snapping, position snaps but rotation does not align; with Face snapping plus Align Rotation to Target but not Project Individual Elements, rotation aligns but behaves inconsistently; with all three plus a temporary snap hold (Ctrl) while moving (G), the object snaps cleanly to the surface in both position and orientation.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript [1:01:47-1:02:21]: 'Now enable snapping, or you can also hold down CTRL to temporarily enable this... and then let's enable face snapping. What this does, when I know hold down CTRL and move the object, It will snap to the faces. But you can see the rotation will not align, so let's also enable, align rotation to target, which is already better, but still acts a bit weird as you can see, and to fix that, click up here and enable project individual elements. And now if I hit G to move it and CTRL to temporarily enable snapping, you can see it will perfectly snap to the surface.' Precondition per [1:01:28-1:01:47]: the object's local Z axis should point toward the target surface and its origin should sit low on the object -- if the object's rotation isn't already applied, apply it first (Ctrl+A > Rotation).
rejected_alternative: Manually eyeballing position and rotation to seat a secondary part (e.g. a bolt) against a curved host surface, or reaching for a Shrinkwrap modifier as the only conforming mechanism.
reason: This is a real-time, interactive, non-destructive alternative to a Shrinkwrap-Project modifier for conforming a secondary part's placement to a curved host, relevant to this project's already-flagged untested Shrinkwrap hypothesis for the mug's handle-attachment problem. It only snaps at the moment of placement rather than keeping the part continuously conformed if the host mesh changes afterward, so it suits one-off placement (e.g. scattering bolts) rather than a part that must stay glued to a surface through later edits.

claim: Alt+D creates a 'linked duplicate': a separate object that shares the same mesh data-block as the source object (visible in the Outliner as both objects referencing the same mesh name). Editing the mesh in Edit Mode on either object updates all linked duplicates simultaneously. Modifiers are NOT linked -- each linked-duplicate object keeps its own independent modifier stack, so per-instance variation is still possible while the base geometry stays shared.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript [1:02:41-1:03:26]: 'you can also duplicate an object with ALT + D, this will create a linked duplicate... we have two different objects here in object mode, but when I switch to edit mode, both elements will use the same mesh... If I click on this and make one change on one of these objects, the other one will change as well. One additional info here, modifiers won't be linked. That means if I have some modifiers here, I can change them individually on all these objects, which can also help to create variations of the same object.'
rejected_alternative: Regular duplicate (Shift+D), which creates a fully independent mesh copy per instance -- correct when true independence is needed, but wasteful (larger file, no shared-edit propagation) for many identical repeated parts like bolts or panel rivets that should all update together whenever the base shape is refined.
reason: Directly relevant to modular kitbash-style construction of repeated hardware: editing one instance's geometry in Edit Mode propagates to every linked duplicate at once, while each instance can still carry its own modifier-level variation (e.g. a different bevel amount or array count).

claim: Objects that were duplicated independently (Shift+D, not sharing mesh data) can be retroactively converted to share a mesh: select all the objects that should share it, select last (making active) the one object whose mesh should become the shared source, then Ctrl+L > Object Data. This makes every other selected object reference the active object's mesh data-block, behaving from then on exactly like a set of Alt+D linked duplicates.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript [1:03:52-1:04:19]: 'what if you forgot to hit ALT + D, and pressed SHIFT+D a few times, and then realizing, okay, all these meshes are not linked to each other. How can we change this? Simply select all the objects and as the last object, the one from which you want to link the mesh to all the other ones, and simply hit CTLR + L and click on object data. Now, the mesh from this object was linked to all the other ones here.'
rejected_alternative: Deleting and redoing all the duplicates as Alt+D linked duplicates from scratch after realizing the mistake, discarding any per-instance positioning or rotation already done.
reason: A recovery path for exactly the scenario of accidentally using independent duplicates (Shift+D) for what should have been shared hardware instances -- lets shared-mesh editing be adopted after the fact without redoing placement work.

claim: To edit a mesh that currently sits in an inconvenient transform state (e.g. rotated or animated into an odd orientation) without disturbing that placement: Alt+D a linked duplicate of it, reset the duplicate's rotation and position (Alt+R, Alt+G) so it sits conveniently at the origin, edit the duplicate's geometry in Edit Mode, then delete the duplicate object. Because the duplicate shared mesh data with the original, the edits already exist on the original's data-block too -- the original keeps its awkward transform but now carries the edited geometry.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript [1:04:34-1:05:19]: 'editing something, which is weirdly rotated is always a bit inconvenient... what we can do, we can make use of linked duplicate. So let's ALT + D, duplicate this, press, ALT + R, ALT + G to reset the rotation and position. Now let's make the changes here... And now when I go back to object mode all those changes I made over here are now also done over here on this original object. That means we can simply delete the duplicate and all the changes here, stay intact.'
rejected_alternative: Moving/rotating the original object itself into a convenient pose to edit it, making the changes, then trying to manually restore its exact original transform values afterward -- error-prone, especially if the original transform was itself animated rather than a single static value.
reason: A genuine choice between two edit strategies with a stated reason in the transcript: transforming the original risks losing or mis-restoring a load-bearing (possibly animated) transform, whereas spawning a disposable linked-duplicate proxy at a convenient pose exploits shared mesh data to edit geometry without ever touching the original's transform at all.

claim: To make one object's location and rotation exactly match another's: select the object(s) that should receive the copy first, then Shift-click the source object last so it becomes the active object. In the N-panel's Item tab, right-click the Location field and choose 'Copy All to Selected' (or copy a single axis), then do the same on the Rotation field. This copies the active object's origin-based location/rotation onto every other selected object. Local transform orientation must be consistent between the objects for the copied rotation to align them as expected, since the operation copies the source origin's coordinates onto the target origin.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript [1:06:16-1:06:58]: 'I wanna copy the location and rotation of this object, to this object... For doing that, simply select the one first, where you wanna copy the information to, and then, SHIFT select the object where you wanna copy the information from. Make sure that with N, the sidebars open, under item, you find the transform panel and then simply right click on the location, and then you can either copy the single information from, for example, the Y axis to the selected object or copy all which I use in this case... and then right click on rotation, copy all to select it.' Caveat at [1:07:02-1:07:18]: 'it's important that the local transform orientation is correct... it will use the origin of the object and copies the coordinates of this to the origin of the other object.'
rejected_alternative: Manually reading the source object's X/Y/Z location and rotation values off the N-panel and retyping them into the target object's fields one at a time.
reason: A precise, error-free way to make two objects' origins coincide in position and rotation -- useful whenever a secondary part's origin needs to exactly match a reference or mounting point on another object, though it aligns origin-to-origin rather than conforming a footprint to a curved surface the way Snap-to-Surface or a Shrinkwrap modifier do.
